notes.definition: Metallic bonding is the strong attraction between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons shared through a giant metallic structure.
explanation: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern, usually in closely packed layers. The electrons in the outer shell of each metal atom are not held by that atom. Instead they are delocalised, which means they are free to move through the whole structure. When an atom loses its outer electrons into this shared 'sea' of electrons, what is left behind is a positive metal ion. For example, each sodium atom (2,8,1) releases one electron and becomes Na⁺; each magnesium atom (2,8,2) releases two electrons and becomes Mg²⁺.

The sharing of delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds. The bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the negatively charged delocalised electrons around them. Because the electrons are spread throughout the structure, the attraction acts in all directions, and each ion is held by the electrons around it rather than by one fixed bond to a particular neighbour. Metallic bonding is found in metallic elements and also in alloys, which are mixtures of metals (or of a metal with small amounts of other elements).

Metallic bonding is usually represented by a diagram showing positive metal ions arranged in regular rows, surrounded by delocalised electrons drawn as e⁻ or as small dots. You should be able to label the positive ions and the delocalised electrons and explain what each represents. Like all models, the diagram has limitations: it is two-dimensional, it shows only a tiny part of a giant structure, and it shows the electrons in fixed positions when in fact they are constantly moving throughout the metal.

The model of metallic bonding helps to explain the properties of metals, which you will study in more detail later. Strong metallic bonds mean that a lot of energy is needed to separate the ions, so most metals have high melting and boiling points. The delocalised electrons can move through the structure and carry charge and energy, so metals are good conductors of electricity and thermal energy. The regular layers of ions can slide over each other, so pure metals can be bent and shaped.
keyFacts: Metals are giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
The outer shell electrons of metal atoms are delocalised.
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole structure.
Losing outer electrons to the 'sea' leaves positive metal ions.
Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
The sharing of delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.
Na releases 1 electron per atom (Na⁺); Mg releases 2 (Mg²⁺); Al releases 3 (Al³⁺).

keyTerms.definition: The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons around them.
An electron that is not attached to a particular atom or bond and is free to move through the whole structure.
A structure containing a very large number of particles arranged in a regular, repeating pattern.
What remains of a metal atom after its outer shell electrons have become delocalised.
A mixture of a metal with at least one other element; alloys are held together by metallic bonding.
A description of the delocalised electrons that surround the positive ions in a metal.

workedExamples.title: Describing metallic bonding in magnesium
workedExamples.question: Describe the structure and bonding in magnesium. Magnesium has electronic structure 2,8,2.
steps: Magnesium is a metal, so it has a giant structure of atoms arranged in a regular pattern (layers).
Each atom's 2 outer shell electrons become delocalised.
The delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole structure.
There is a strong electrostatic attraction between the Mg²⁺ ions and the delocalised electrons: the metallic bond.
workedExamples.answer: Giant regular structure of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (2 per atom), held by strong electrostatic attraction.

workedExamples.title: Counting delocalised electrons
workedExamples.question: A tiny piece of aluminium contains 5000 atoms. Aluminium is in Group 3. How many delocalised electrons are there, and what is the charge on each ion?
steps: Aluminium is in Group 3, so each atom has 3 outer electrons.
All 3 become delocalised, leaving Al³⁺ ions.
Check: total positive charge = 5000 × 3+ = 15 000+, which balances the 15 000 electrons, so the metal is neutral overall.
workedExamples.answer: 15 000 delocalised electrons; each ion is Al³⁺

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals contain negative ions as well as positive ions.
misconceptions.right: Metals contain positive ions only; the negative charge comes from the delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the delocalised electrons belong to particular atoms.
misconceptions.right: Delocalised electrons are shared by the whole structure and are free to move anywhere in it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often describe metallic bonding as ionic bonding because ions are involved.
misconceptions.right: Ionic bonding is between oppositely charged ions. Metallic bonding is between positive ions and delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metallic bonds are weak because metals can be bent.
misconceptions.right: Metallic bonds are strong. Metals can be bent because layers of ions can slide while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together.

realWorld: Copper is used in electrical wiring because its delocalised electrons move through the metal and carry the current.
Tungsten has very strong metallic bonding and an extremely high melting point, so it was used for light bulb filaments.
Steel and brass are alloys held together by metallic bonding and are used for construction and fittings.
examTips: Use the full phrase: 'strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons'.
Say 'delocalised electrons', not 'free ions' or 'free atoms'. Only electrons move freely.
When labelling a diagram, label the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons (the 'sea of electrons').
Do not mention negative ions or shared pairs when describing metals.
summary: Metals are giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
Outer shell electrons are delocalised and free to move through the whole structure.
This leaves positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
Metallic bonds are the strong attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
Metallic bonding is found in metal elements and alloys.

flashcards.front: Describe the structure of a metal.
flashcards.back: A giant structure of atoms (positive ions) arranged in a regular pattern.

flashcards.front: What happens to the outer shell electrons of metal atoms?
flashcards.back: They become delocalised and free to move through the whole structure.
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Not attached to any one atom; free to move through the whole structure.

flashcards.front: Are metallic bonds strong or weak?
What two things should you label on a metallic bonding diagram?
flashcards.back: Positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

flashcards.front: Limitation of a metallic bonding diagram?
flashcards.back: It is 2D, shows only a small part of the structure and shows moving electrons in fixed positions.

flashcards.front: Are there negative ions in a metal?
flashcards.back: No. The negative charge is carried by the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: What type of structure do metals have?
options: Giant structure of atoms in a regular pattern
markScheme: 1 mark: Giant structure of atoms in a regular pattern
questions.explanation: Metals are giant structures of atoms (positive ions) arranged in a regular pattern.

questions.question: Which particles are free to move through a metal structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: The outer shell electrons are delocalised and free to move. The positive ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice (they can vibrate).

questions.question: Metallic bonding is the attraction between:
options: positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
shared pairs of electrons and nuclei of two atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metallic bonds are between positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. Option A is ionic and option C is covalent.

questions.question: Which electrons in a metal atom become delocalised?
options: The electrons in the inner shell
The electrons in the outer shell
markScheme: 1 mark: The electrons in the outer shell
questions.explanation: Only the outer shell electrons are delocalised. Inner shell electrons stay with the ion; there are no electrons in the nucleus.

questions.question: What is the charge on the ions in calcium metal? Calcium is in Group 2.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2+
questions.explanation: Each calcium atom releases its 2 outer electrons into the sea of delocalised electrons, leaving Ca²⁺ ions.

questions.question: Which substance has metallic bonding?
markScheme: 1 mark: Steel
questions.explanation: Steel is an alloy of iron, and alloys have metallic bonding. Sodium chloride is ionic; silicon dioxide and carbon dioxide are covalent.

questions.question: Why are metallic bonds described as strong?
options: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
There is a strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
Each atom shares a pair of electrons with one neighbour.
The ions are held by intermolecular forces.
markScheme: 1 mark: There is a strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
questions.explanation: The strong attraction between the positive ions and the sea of negative electrons holds the structure together.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why a metal has no overall charge?
options: The number of delocalised electrons balances the total charge on the positive ions.
The delocalised electrons have no charge.
Each metal ion is paired with a negative ion.
markScheme: 1 mark: The number of delocalised electrons balances the total charge on the positive ions.
questions.explanation: Every electron released leaves one positive charge on an ion, so the total negative charge of the electrons equals the total positive charge.

questions.question: A student draws a metal as positive ions and negative ions in alternating rows. What is wrong with the diagram?
options: The ions should be shown as molecules.
There are no negative ions in a metal; the negative charge is from delocalised electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: There are no negative ions in a metal; the negative charge is from delocalised electrons.
questions.explanation: Alternating positive and negative ions describes an ionic lattice. A metal is positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Which is a limitation of the usual diagram of metallic bonding?
options: It shows the ions in a regular arrangement.
It shows electrons in fixed positions, although they move throughout the structure.
It shows that the electrons are shared by many ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: It shows electrons in fixed positions, although they move throughout the structure.
questions.explanation: The electrons are constantly moving; a still diagram cannot show this. The other options are things the diagram shows correctly.

questions.question: How many delocalised electrons does each sodium atom provide in sodium metal? Sodium is in Group 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1
questions.explanation: Sodium has one outer shell electron (2,8,1), which becomes delocalised.

questions.question: How many delocalised electrons does each aluminium atom provide in aluminium metal? Aluminium is in Group 3.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3
questions.explanation: Aluminium (2,8,3) has three outer electrons; all become delocalised, leaving Al³⁺ ions.

questions.question: A sample of magnesium contains 600 atoms. How many delocalised electrons does it contain? Magnesium is in Group 2.
questions.explanation: Each magnesium atom releases 2 electrons: 600 × 2 = 1200.

questions.question: Sodium has atomic number 11. How many electrons remain on each ion in sodium metal (not counting the delocalised electrons)?
markScheme: 1 mark: one electron per atom is delocalised
questions.explanation: A sodium atom has 11 electrons. One becomes delocalised, leaving Na⁺ with 10 electrons (2,8).

questions.question: Describe the structure of a metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant structure of atoms / positive ions in a regular pattern (layers)
1 mark: with delocalised electrons (sea of electrons)
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: the regular arrangement of positive ions and the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: State what is meant by a delocalised electron.
markScheme: 1 mark: an electron that is not attached to a particular atom and is free to move through the structure
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are shared by the whole metal structure.

questions.question: Name the two types of particle shown in a diagram of metallic bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: positive (metal) ions
1 mark: delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metal diagrams show positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Explain what holds the particles together in a metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: strong (electrostatic) attraction
1 mark: between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: This attraction is the metallic bond; it acts throughout the structure.

questions.question: Explain why the particles in a metal are described as positive ions rather than atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: the outer shell electrons have been released / become delocalised
1 mark: so each particle has more protons than electrons / is positively charged
questions.explanation: Once the outer electrons leave to join the sea of electrons, each remaining particle is positive.

questions.question: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. State and explain the type of bonding in brass.
markScheme: 1 mark: metallic bonding
1 mark: positive (copper and zinc) ions held by attraction to delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Alloys of metals have the same type of bonding as the pure metals.

questions.question: Suggest why the metallic bonding in magnesium is stronger than in sodium.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium ions have a higher charge (2+ compared with 1+)
1 mark: there are more delocalised electrons per atom, so the attraction is stronger
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ ions and twice as many delocalised electrons give a stronger electrostatic attraction, which is why magnesium has a higher melting point (650 °C) than sodium (98 °C).

questions.question: Compare metallic bonding with ionic bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: similarity: both involve strong electrostatic attraction / both contain positive metal ions
1 mark: in ionic bonding the positive ions attract negative ions
1 mark: in metallic bonding the positive ions attract delocalised electrons (and there are no negative ions)
questions.explanation: Both are electrostatic, but the negative charge is on non-metal ions in ionic compounds and on delocalised electrons in metals.

questions.question: Give two limitations of a 2D diagram of metallic bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: only shows two dimensions / one layer; shows only a small part of the giant structure; shows electrons in fixed positions when they move; sizes / spacing not to scale
questions.explanation: Diagrams are simplified models; real metals are 3D and contain huge numbers of moving electrons.

questions.question: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal such as copper. You may refer to a labelled diagram in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: giant structure; atoms arranged in a regular pattern / layers; outer shell electrons delocalised; free to move through the whole structure; leaving positive metal ions; strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons; diagram labelled with positive ions and delocalised electrons (sea of electrons).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): accurate description of both the structure and the bonding using the terms positive ions, delocalised electrons and electrostatic attraction
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct points, for example 'sea of electrons' or 'positive ions', with little explanation of the attraction
questions.explanation: Answers need both structure (giant, regular, positive ions) and bonding (strong attraction to delocalised electrons).

questions.question:
Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals in the same period. Their melting points are: sodium 98 °C, magnesium 650 °C, aluminium 660 °C.
Explain metallic bonding and use the model to suggest why the strength of metallic bonding differs between these three metals.
markScheme: Indicative content: metals have giant structures of atoms in regular layers; outer shell electrons are delocalised and free to move; leaving positive metal ions; metallic bond is strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons; sodium releases 1 electron per atom (Na⁺), magnesium 2 (Mg²⁺), aluminium 3 (Al³⁺); more delocalised electrons and higher charge on ions gives stronger attraction; more energy needed to overcome the bonds when melting; so sodium has the weakest metallic bonding and lowest melting point; magnesium and aluminium have stronger bonding and much higher melting points; the model does not fully explain why aluminium's melting point is only slightly higher than magnesium's, as other factors are involved.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear description of metallic bonding linked logically to the number of delocalised electrons and ion charge, used to explain the trend in the data
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct description of metallic bonding with some attempt to link the number of delocalised electrons or ion charge to the melting points
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about delocalised electrons or positive ions, or a description of the data with little explanation
questions.explanation: The best answers explain the model first, then apply it: more delocalised electrons per atom and a higher ion charge mean stronger attraction, so more energy is needed to melt the metal.

questions.question: Explain why the term 'sea of electrons' is used to describe the electrons in a metal, and why the metal stays together even though the electrons move.
markScheme: Indicative content: outer shell electrons leave their atoms; spread throughout the whole structure like a sea; free to move in any direction / delocalised; positive ions are surrounded by the negative electrons on all sides; strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the electrons in all directions; this attraction holds the ions in place even as individual electrons move.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of why the electrons are described as a sea and how the attraction in all directions holds the structure together
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a basic description of moving or shared electrons with little explanation
questions.explanation: The electrons are not in fixed bonds, but there are always electrons surrounding each ion, so the attraction is maintained.
